title: Flight power bank
topic: A friend converts a power bank's rated capacity into 20%-to-100% phone top-ups
blurb: 20,000 mAh at 65% efficiency, 4,000 mAh phone topped from 20% to 100% — four full charges?
prompt: A friend texted this while packing for a long-haul flight. Tap a line if the battery math breaks, or call it clean.

segments.label: The pack
segments.text: Packed a 20,000 mAh power bank for the flight; the fine print says usable output after conversion is about 65%, so roughly 13,000 mAh actually reaches the phone.

segments.label: The phone
segments.text: My phone battery is 4,000 mAh, and I usually plug in whenever it hits 20% and charge it back to 100%.

segments.label: The count
segments.text: Each 80% top-up needs 3,200 mAh, so 13,000 mAh gives me four full top-ups with a tiny bit left over.

segments.label: The relief
segments.text: No need to fight my seatmate for the outlet.

conclusion: 13,000 mAh usable output divided by 3,200 mAh per 80% top-up gives four top-ups with 200 mAh to spare.

diagnosis: 65% of 20,000 mAh is 12,000 mAh, not 13,000 mAh — you rounded the efficiency up.
A 20,000 mAh pack loses 65% in conversion, leaving only 7,000 mAh usable output.
Airlines ban 20,000 mAh power banks in carry-on bags, so you can't even bring it on the flight.
You can't take 65% of mAh directly without multiplying by 5V first, which cuts usable output in half.
fix: Fix 20,000 × 0.65 to 12,000 mAh, which is less than four top-ups.
Take the remaining 35% (7,000 mAh) as usable output instead of 65%.
Leave the 20,000 mAh pack at home and pack a 10,000 mAh one for TSA.
Divide 13,000 mAh by 1.35 again for the 3.7V-to-5V boost step.

diagnosis: Charging from 20% to 100% still takes 100% of the battery's 4,000 mAh because the last 20% trickles slowly.
Plugging in at 20% means you only have 20% left to fill, not 80%.
A 4,000 mAh phone charged from 20% to 100% still pulls 65% extra loss on top of line 1.
Using the phone while charging doesn't count against the 4,000 mAh battery size.
fix: Budget a full 4,000 mAh per charge so you only get three top-ups.
Apply the 65% conversion loss a second time to the phone's 3,200 mAh.
Stop charging at 80% instead of 100% to save power.
Count 20% to 100% as 3,600 mAh to cover trickle-charge overhead.

diagnosis: Four times 3,200 is 13,800 mAh, which is 800 mAh more than 13,000 — you only get three full top-ups.
80% of 4,000 mAh is 3,400 mAh, so four top-ups need 13,600 mAh and come up short.
13,000 divided by 4,000 is 3.25 — you can't get four top-ups out of a pack that only holds 3.25 phone batteries.
You forgot to apply the 65% efficiency to the 3,200 mAh figure, which makes each top-up cost ~4,920 mAh.
fix: Recheck 4 × 3,200 = 13,800 mAh and plan for three full top-ups instead of four.
Divide 13,000 by the full 4,000 mAh phone capacity: 3.25 charges, not 4.
Divide 3,200 by 0.65 (≈ 4,923 mAh) — you only get two full top-ups.
Fix 80% of 4,000 to 3,400 mAh and count three top-ups.

diagnosis: Since 4 × 3,200 is 13,800 mAh, you'll run dry on the fourth charge and still need the seat outlet.
With only 200 mAh left over, even a tiny bit of screen-on drain during charging means you won't finish the fourth top-up.
Three top-ups at 4,000 mAh each leaves you short on a 14-hour flight.
A 20,000 mAh pack takes 6 hours to recharge, so you'll still want the outlet on the return leg.
fix: Grab the seat outlet for the first charge so the pack covers the rest.
Switch to airplane mode while charging so the 200 mAh margin doesn't evaporate.
Pack a second cable in case the seat outlet is needed for charge four.
Plan for three top-ups instead of four so you aren't caught at 10%.

clean_segments: Packed a 20,000 mAh power bank for the flight; the fine print says usable output after conversion is about 65%, so roughly 13,000 mAh actually reaches the phone.
My phone battery is 4,000 mAh, and I usually plug in whenever it hits 20% and charge it back to 100%.
Each 80% top-up needs 3,200 mAh, so 13,000 mAh gives me four full top-ups with a tiny bit left over.
No need to fight my seatmate for the outlet.
clean_conclusion: All three steps hold up: 65% of 20,000 is 13,000 mAh; 80% of 4,000 is 3,200 mAh; and 4 × 3,200 = 12,800 mAh, leaving 200 mAh to spare.
